zh.summary: 用同一收件任務區分人機互動、介面與整體使用經驗，找到該改善的問題與需要的證據。
objectives: 以工作情境區分 HCI、UI 與 UX 的分析範圍。
指出美觀、易用與整體任務結果之間的差異。
為一個介面困難提出可觀察的修改假設。

readingGuide.goal: 以工作情境區分 HCI、UI 與 UX 的分析範圍。
readingGuide.startingPoint: problem.md、文字編輯器與合成收件情境；不需要改程式或接觸真人。
readingGuide.route: 先看情境與原理，再比較例子，最後擴寫 wireframe-notes.md 並用檢核題自查。
readingGuide.output: 一份包含三種分析觀點、具體修改假設及待驗方法的 wireframe-notes.md。

sections.heading: 讓使用者理解系統並完成工作
paragraphs: 這堂課最重要的觀念是：
設計一套系統，不是為了讓畫面漂亮，而是要讓使用者能理解系統、正確操作，最後完成真正的工作。
HCI、UI、UX 就是從三個不同角度，檢查這件事情有沒有做好。

sections.heading: 一、先用餐廳點餐機理解
paragraphs: 想像你到麥當勞，使用自助點餐機。
你希望的是什麼？不是欣賞點餐機的設計，而是能夠快速點到想吃的東西、付錢、拿到餐點。
但這個簡單的過程，其實可以分成三個問題。

blocks.heading: UI：畫面怎麼呈現？
paragraphs: 點餐機上的漢堡圖片、價格、數量、結帳按鈕、返回上一頁，都是 UI（User Interface）。
例如，結帳按鈕太小、字體看不清楚、價格藏在不明顯的位置，這些就是 UI 設計問題。

blocks.heading: HCI：人如何理解和操作機器？
paragraphs: 假設你看到一個「完成」按鈕。
你可能以為按下去就完成付款，但實際上只是完成餐點選擇。
這時問題不只是按鈕長得如何，而是：為什麼使用者會這樣理解？
HCI（Human–Computer Interaction）研究人的認知、行為、操作能力與技術之間的互動。
例如，老人家看得懂嗎？使用輪椅的人能不能碰到按鈕？使用者是否知道下一步要做什麼？

blocks.heading: UX：整段過程到底好不好？
paragraphs: 假設你非常順利地點完餐、付款成功，卻不知道去哪裡領餐。
這時候點餐機可能非常好用，整體體驗卻很差。
UX（User Experience）要考慮的不只是點餐機，還包含進店、點餐、付款、等待、領餐，甚至遇到問題如何處理。

sections.heading: 二、用一張表記住三者的差別
paragraphs: 用各自關心的問題比較三種觀點，較容易判斷要檢查什麼。

blocks.caption: 表 1｜三種觀點的差別
rows: HCI 人機互動
研究人怎麼理解、使用科技
人為什麼會這樣操作？
UI 使用者介面
人看得到、操作得到的介面
按鈕、文字、提示應該怎麼設計？
UX 使用者經驗
從開始到完成的整體體驗
最後有沒有順利完成工作？

paragraphs: 要特別注意：這不是三個互不相關的盒子。
HCI 是跨領域的研究與設計領域；UI 是人與系統互動的接觸介面；UX 則是整體使用經驗。三者彼此重疊、互相影響。

sections.heading: 三、回到我們正在設計的收件系統
paragraphs: 假設現在要開發一個簡單的網頁，讓承辦人員檢查資料是否齊全，再匯出報告。
原本流程是：

blocks.caption: 圖 1｜原本的收件流程
blocks.description: 四個步驟依序進行；「顯示成功」尚未說明成功的範圍。

paragraphs: 現在出現一個問題：承辦人看到「成功」，以為案件已經正式受理。
但系統其實只確認三個必要欄位已填寫。
這就是很典型的設計問題。

blocks.caption: 圖 2｜從 HCI、UI、UX 檢查收件系統
blocks.description: 三種觀點互相影響，並列呈現，不表示先後階段。

items.title: HCI：研究為什麼會誤解
items.body:
使用者心目中的「成功」是什麼意思？他是否知道欄位齊全和正式受理不同？

可以請他直接說明畫面意思，而不是由開發者自行猜測。

items.title: UI：修改畫面上呈現的資訊
items.body:
不要只顯示「成功」，而要說明具體完成了什麼。

例如：「三個必要欄位已齊全，尚未正式送件。」

同時提供清楚的下一步操作。

items.title: UX：確認整段工作是否順利
items.body:
即使畫面讓人看懂了，承辦人匯出報告後，究竟應該交給誰？接手者能不能使用？

如果接手者還得重新輸入全部資料，整體工作流程仍然有問題。

sections.heading: 四、直接看一個 UI 修改的實例
paragraphs: 以下是示意畫面，不是真實系統或測試結果。

blocks.caption: 圖 3｜狀態提示的修改前與候選修改
blocks.description: 示意畫面，不是真實系統或測試結果；候選修改仍需要驗證。

items.title: 修改前
items.body:
成功！

操作完成

確定

沒有解釋成功的是什麼，也不知道下一步。

items.title: 候選修改
items.body:
欄位檢查完成

3 個必要欄位已齊全。

尚未正式受理，請依程序辦理送件。

匯出檢查報告

明確說明狀態，以及接下來能做什麼。

paragraphs: 這個修改看起來比較清楚，但有一個非常重要的科學觀念：
設計者覺得比較清楚，不代表使用者真的理解得比較好。
所以還需要驗證。

sections.heading: 五、如何證明真的改善了？
paragraphs: 把「改善 UX」當成一項需要證據的設計工作。

blocks.caption: 表 2｜問題與驗證方法
rows: 使用者看懂「欄位齊全」嗎？
請他用自己的話解釋目前狀態
使用者知道如何補件嗎？
給他一個缺件情境，觀察是否能找到欄位並修正
不使用滑鼠能操作嗎？
實際用鍵盤 Tab、Enter 等完成操作
接手者拿到報告後能繼續工作嗎？
讓接手角色用報告完成指定的後續任務

paragraphs: 這裡還有一個差別：

- 功能正確： 程式有沒有照規則運作？
- 易用性（Usability）： 使用者能不能有效、有效率地完成指定任務？
- UX： 包含使用前、使用中、使用後，整體感受與結果如何？
例如，100 次缺件測試全部成功擋住，能支持程式在這些案例下的檢查邏輯正確，卻不能證明 100 位使用者都能理解錯誤提示。

sections.heading: 六、以後請 AI 設計介面，應該怎麼提需求？
paragraphs: 以前可能只會說：
> 請幫我把這個網頁做得更漂亮，改善 UX。
這種指令會讓 AI 自行決定什麼叫改善，可能只是換顏色、增加動畫和陰影。
比較好的做法，是描述五件事：

blocks.caption: 圖 4｜一個可驗證的設計需求
blocks.description: 誰使用 → 做什麼 → 遇到什麼困難 → 要如何修改 → 怎麼驗證

items.title: 使用者
items.body: 第一次使用系統的承辦人

items.title: 任務
items.body: 找出缺少的文件類型並補正

items.title: 候選修改
items.body: 在欄位旁顯示具體錯誤與修正指引

items.title: 驗證方法
items.body: 指定缺件情境，觀察使用者是否能自行修正

paragraphs: 這就是從「要求 AI 美化」轉成「要求 AI 解決可驗證的使用問題」。
在還沒測試之前，只能稱為設計假設，不能說已經驗證有效。

sections.heading: 七、這一課與下一課有什麼關係？
paragraphs: 今天 M04-01 學的是用 HCI、UI、UX 三個角度發現問題。
下一課 M04-02「Task Analysis（任務分析）」則會更進一步，把真正的工作拆開：

blocks.caption: 圖 5｜把真正的工作拆成任務
blocks.description: 依序檢查每一步的角色、資訊、成功條件與例外。

paragraphs: 任務分析不是一開始就畫畫面，而是先問：每一步是誰做的、需要什麼資訊、如何判斷成功，以及出了問題該怎麼辦？
理解這些之後再設計線框稿（Wireframe），才比較不容易做出「畫面很好看，但實際工作無法完成」的系統。

sections.heading: 理解檢核
paragraphs: 請先嘗試回答以下三題，不需要使用專業術語。
請先自行作答，再展開下方的參考解析核對理由。
這堂課先掌握一句話：UI 是人操作系統的介面，HCI 幫我們理解人與系統如何互動，UX 則提醒我們不能忘記使用者真正要完成的整段工作。

exercise.environment: problem.md、文字編輯器與合成收件情境；不需要改程式或接觸真人。
steps: 用同一缺件任務各寫一個 HCI、UI 與 UX 問題，保留操作前後的情境。
選一項困難，提出介面修改假設，說明要用什麼證據判斷。
將假設放入 wireframe-notes.md，和同儕核對是否把美觀或程式通過誤當成整體任務改善；單人可依檢核題自查。
exercise.expected: 一份包含三種分析觀點、具體修改假設及待驗方法的 wireframe-notes.md。
exercise.check: 能解釋三種觀點如何重疊；每個問題都有可觀察情境，沒有虛構研究結果。
exercise.cleanup: 保留合成標記與未知，移除真人姓名、案件內容與沒有用途的個人描述。

openChecks.prompt: 使用者看見「成功」，卻誤以為案件已經送出。你會先從 HCI、UI、UX 的哪個角度研究原因？為什麼？
answer: 先從 HCI 研究使用者如何理解「成功」以及為何誤判。請他用自己的話解釋狀態，找出「欄位齊全」與「正式送出」的認知差異；再以 UI 改寫狀態與下一步，並從 UX 檢查送件流程。三者互相影響。

openChecks.prompt: 系統介面簡潔、按鈕明顯，使用者也能匯出報告，但接手者仍要全部重填。問題主要出在哪個層面？
answer: 主要從 UX 檢查整段工作與交接。單一介面能操作、能匯出，仍不足以讓接手者完成後續任務；需要查看報告缺少什麼資訊或格式，以及交接規則。

openChecks.prompt: AI 幫你重新設計缺件提示，畫面更漂亮、訊息也更具體。接下來要取得什麼證據，才能說這項修改確實有幫助？
answer: 給使用者指定的缺件情境，觀察他能否找到欄位、說明缺漏並自行修正；記錄提示、錯誤與任務結果，再依同等條件比較修改前後。漂亮與具體的文字仍是候選設計，程式測試也不能代替人的理解證據。

en.summary: Use one intake task to distinguish human–computer interaction, the interface and the overall user experience, identifying problems to improve and the evidence needed.
objectives: Distinguish the scope of HCI, UI and UX through a work situation.
Identify differences among appearance, usability and overall task outcomes.
Propose an observable design hypothesis for an interface difficulty.

readingGuide.goal: Distinguish the scope of HCI, UI and UX through a work situation.
readingGuide.startingPoint: problem.md, a text editor and a synthetic intake scenario; no code changes or actual participants are needed.
readingGuide.route: Read the situation and principles, compare examples, then expand wireframe-notes.md and use the checks to review your understanding.
readingGuide.output: wireframe-notes.md with three analytical perspectives, a concrete design hypothesis and a planned verification method.

sections.heading: Help users understand the system and complete their work
paragraphs: The main idea of this lesson is:
Design a system so people can understand it, operate it correctly and complete their actual work; an attractive screen alone does not achieve that goal.
HCI, UI and UX provide three perspectives for checking whether the design achieves it.

sections.heading: 1. Start with a restaurant ordering kiosk
paragraphs: Imagine ordering at a McDonald’s self-service kiosk.
You want to choose your food quickly, pay and collect your meal. Admiring the kiosk’s design is not the purpose of your visit.
This simple process raises three questions.

blocks.heading: UI: how is the screen presented?
paragraphs: The burger images, prices, quantities, checkout button and back control are all parts of the UI (User Interface).
A checkout button that is too small, unreadable text or a price hidden in an obscure location are UI design problems.

blocks.heading: HCI: how do people understand and operate the machine?
paragraphs: Suppose you see a button labeled “Done.”
You might think pressing it completes payment, although it only finishes meal selection.
The question extends beyond the button’s appearance: why does the user interpret it that way?
HCI (Human–Computer Interaction) studies interactions between people’s cognition, behavior, operating abilities and technology.
Can an older person understand the screen? Can a wheelchair user reach the buttons? Does the user know what to do next?

blocks.heading: UX: how does the whole process work out?
paragraphs: Suppose you select and pay for your meal smoothly but do not know where to collect it.
The kiosk may be easy to use while the overall experience is poor.
UX (User Experience) considers entering the restaurant, ordering, paying, waiting, collecting the meal and getting help when something goes wrong, as well as the kiosk itself.

sections.heading: 2. Compare the three perspectives in one table
paragraphs: Compare the questions each perspective asks to decide what to examine.

blocks.caption: Table 1 | Compare the perspectives
rows: HCI: human–computer interaction
Studies how people understand and use technology
Why does the person operate it this way?
UI: user interface
The interface people perceive and operate
How should buttons, text and feedback be designed?
UX: user experience
The overall experience from starting to finishing
Can the person complete the actual work smoothly?

paragraphs: These are not three independent boxes.

HCI is an interdisciplinary research and design field; UI is the contact interface between a person and a system; UX is the overall experience of use. The perspectives overlap and influence one another.

sections.heading: 3. Return to the intake system we are designing
paragraphs: Suppose we are developing a simple web page that lets a case worker check whether information is complete and export a report.
The original process is:

blocks.caption: Figure 1 | The original intake process
blocks.description: Four steps proceed in order; “Success” does not specify what has succeeded.

paragraphs: A problem appears: the case worker sees “Success” and assumes the case has been officially accepted.
The system has only confirmed that three required fields are filled in.
This is a typical design problem.

blocks.caption: Figure 2 | Examine intake through HCI, UI and UX
blocks.description: The perspectives influence one another and are presented in parallel, not as successive phases.

items.title: HCI: investigate the misunderstanding
items.body:
What does “success” mean to the user? Do they know that complete fields and official acceptance differ?

Ask them to explain the screen directly rather than having developers guess.

items.title: UI: change the information on screen
items.body:
Explain specifically what has been completed instead of only showing “Success.”

For example: “Three required fields are complete; the case has not been formally submitted.”

Provide a clear next action.

items.title: UX: check whether the whole task works
items.body:
Even if the screen is understandable, who should receive the exported report? Can the next worker use it?

If that worker must re-enter all the information, the overall workflow still has a problem.

sections.heading: 4. Examine a UI change directly
paragraphs: These are illustrative screens, not an actual system or test results.

blocks.caption: Figure 3 | Status feedback before and after a candidate change
blocks.description: Illustrative screens, not an actual system or test results; the candidate still needs testing.

items.title: Before
items.body:
Success!

Operation completed

OK

It does not explain what succeeded or what to do next.

items.title: Candidate change
items.body:
Field check completed

3 required fields are complete.

Not officially accepted yet; follow the submission procedure.

Export check report

It states the status and the available next action.

paragraphs: The candidate appears clearer, but the scientific distinction matters:
A designer’s judgment that a screen is clearer does not establish that users understand it better.
The change still needs testing.

sections.heading: 5. How can we establish an improvement?
paragraphs: Treat “improving UX” as design work that requires evidence.

blocks.caption: Table 2 | Questions and verification methods
rows: Do users understand “fields complete”?
Ask them to explain the current state in their own words
Do users know how to supply missing information?
Give them a missing-information scenario and observe whether they find and correct the field
Can they operate without a mouse?
Complete the task using Tab, Enter and other keyboard controls
Can the next worker continue using the report?
Have the receiving role complete a specified follow-up task with it

paragraphs: Also distinguish these concepts:

- Functional correctness: does the program follow its rules?
- Usability: can people complete the specified task effectively and efficiently?
- UX: what are the overall feelings and outcomes before, during and after use?
For example, successfully blocking all 100 missing-input test cases supports the checking logic for those cases. It does not establish that 100 users understand the error message.

sections.heading: 6. How should you ask AI to design an interface?
paragraphs: An earlier request might have been:
> Please make this web page prettier and improve UX.
That request leaves AI to decide what improvement means. It may only change colors, animations and shadows.
A better request describes five things:

blocks.caption: Figure 4 | A verifiable design requirement
blocks.description: Who uses it → what they do → what difficulty they face → what to change → how to test it

items.title: User
items.body: a case worker using the system for the first time

items.title: Task
items.body: identify and correct the missing document type

items.title: Problem
items.body: the user does not know which field is incomplete

items.title: Candidate change
items.body: show a specific error and correction guidance beside the field

items.title: Verification
items.body: give a missing-information scenario and observe whether the user can correct it independently

paragraphs: This changes a request for visual polish into a request to solve an observable usage problem.
Until tested, the candidate remains a design hypothesis; it cannot be described as verified effective.

sections.heading: 7. How does this lesson connect to the next?
paragraphs: M04-01 uses HCI, UI and UX to identify problems from three perspectives.
M04-02, Task Analysis, goes further by breaking down the actual work:

blocks.caption: Figure 5 | Break the actual work into tasks
blocks.description: For each step in order, examine the role, information, success criteria and exceptions.

items.title: Hands it to the next case worker

paragraphs: Task analysis starts by asking who performs each step, what information is needed, how success is judged and what happens when something goes wrong, before drawing screens.
Understanding this work before designing a wireframe reduces the risk of an attractive interface that cannot support the actual task.

sections.heading: Check your understanding
paragraphs: Try these three questions first. You do not need specialist terminology.
Answer independently, then expand the reference explanations below to check your reasoning.
Keep this relationship in mind: UI is the interface people operate; HCI helps us understand interactions between people and systems; UX keeps the whole task the user needs to complete in view.

exercise.environment: problem.md, a text editor and a synthetic intake scenario; no code changes or actual participants are needed.
steps: Write one HCI, UI and UX question for the same missing-information task, retaining its surrounding context.
Choose one difficulty and propose an interface-change hypothesis with evidence to judge it.
Record the hypothesis in wireframe-notes.md. With a peer, check whether appearance or passing code was mistaken for overall task improvement; independent learners can use the checks.
exercise.expected: wireframe-notes.md with three analytical perspectives, a concrete design hypothesis and a planned verification method.
exercise.check: Explain how the perspectives overlap. Every question has an observable situation without invented research results.
exercise.cleanup: Keep synthetic labels and unknowns. Remove actual names, case content and unnecessary personal descriptions.

openChecks.prompt: A user sees “Success” and mistakenly thinks the case has been submitted. Which perspective—HCI, UI or UX—would you first use to investigate the cause, and why?
answer: Start with HCI to investigate how the user interprets “Success” and why the error occurs. Ask them to explain the state in their own words and identify the difference between complete fields and formal submission. Then revise status and next-action wording through UI design and examine the submission workflow through UX. The perspectives interact.

openChecks.prompt: The interface is simple, buttons are clear and users can export reports, but the next worker must re-enter everything. Which perspective mainly reveals the problem?
answer: UX mainly reveals this end-to-end workflow and handoff problem. An operable interface and export function do not ensure that the recipient can complete the next task. Examine missing information or formats in the report and the handoff rules.

openChecks.prompt: AI redesigns missing-information feedback with a prettier screen and more specific wording. What evidence is needed before saying the change helps?
answer: Give users the specified missing-information scenario and observe whether they can locate the field, explain the omission and correct it independently. Record assistance, errors and task outcomes, then compare the earlier and candidate designs under equivalent conditions. Attractive, specific wording remains a candidate; program tests do not replace evidence about human understanding.
